chapters.name: How memory works
chapters.sub: Three stages, a small workbench, and a fast fade

cards.title: Three stages of memory
cards.one: Every memory goes **in**, **stays**, and comes **back out**.

vis.text: Accessing stored information and bringing it back into **awareness**

cards.ex: Remembering a friend's name at a party is retrieval.

cards.title: Working memory is small
cards.one: You can only juggle **a few things** at once, so **group them**.

items: Miller (1956): items people can hold at once
Cowan (2001): a tighter estimate, counted in chunks

say.0: Seven, plus or minus two. Miller's classic estimate of how many items people can hold at once.
say.1: About four. Cowan's tighter estimate, counted in chunks.

vis.title: Chunking
rows: F B I C I A U S A

say.0: Nine separate letters are hard to hold.
say.1: Three familiar chunks are easy. F B I, C I A, U S A.

cards.title: The forgetting curve
cards.one: Forgetting is **fastest right after learning**, then slows down.

say.-1: Ebbinghaus measured how much easier it was to relearn a list later.

vis.text: The drop is **steepest in the first hour**; after that it flattens.

chapters.name: Studying that sticks
chapters.sub: Space it out, test yourself, distrust the glow of rereading

cards.title: The spacing effect
cards.one: The **same study time** works better **spread over days** than crammed into one sitting.

cards.title: The testing effect
cards.one: **Pulling** information out of memory strengthens it more than **reading it again**.

vis.title: Retrieval practice in three steps
items: Write or say what you remember
The effort of recalling is the point

say.0: Tested after five minutes, rereading is slightly ahead.
say.1: Tested after a week, practiced recall is clearly ahead. Roediger and Karpicke, 2006.

cards.hook: Pull it out, don't pour it in

cards.title: The fluency trap
cards.one: Rereading makes material **feel familiar**, and familiarity is easily **mistaken for knowing**.

vis.text: **Familiar is not the same as remembered.** If you can't recall it with the book closed, you don't own it yet.

cards.hook: Close the book to find out

bank.q: Which memory stage means getting stored information **back out**?
bank.exp: Retrieval is accessing stored information. Encoding puts it in; storage keeps it.

bank.q: Chunking lets working memory hold more by grouping items into meaningful units.
bank.exp: Grouping nine letters into three familiar chunks (FBI, CIA, USA) makes them easy to hold.

bank.q: On Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, when is forgetting **fastest**?
bank.exp: Savings fall from about 58% at 20 minutes to 44% at one hour, then the curve flattens.

bank.q: Cramming gives better long-term retention than spacing the same study time.
bank.exp: The spacing effect: the same total time spread over days is retained longer.

bank.q: In Roediger & Karpicke (2006), which group remembered more **a week later**?
opts: Students who practiced recalling the text
bank.exp: Rereading was slightly ahead at five minutes, but practiced recall was clearly ahead after a week.

bank.q: Why can rereading feel effective even when it isn't?
bank.exp: Material you've just reread feels fluent, and that fluency is easily mistaken for being able to recall it.
